options.text: The process of heating a substance until it melts
The process of generating electricity from chemicals
The process of dissolving a substance in water
The process of using electrical energy to decompose an ionic compound

questions.explanation: Electrolysis is the process of using a direct current of electricity to decompose (break down) an ionic compound into its elements. The electrical energy breaks the chemical bonds in the compound.

questions.stem: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved in water for electrolysis to work?

options.text: Because water is needed to produce hydrogen
Because the compound needs to be hot to decompose
Because solid compounds are too heavy
Because the ions must be free to move and carry the electric current

questions.explanation: In a solid ionic compound, the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move. When melted or dissolved, the ions become free to move towards the electrodes and carry the current, allowing electrolysis to occur.

options.text: The battery that provides the electricity
The electrode connected to the positive terminal
The molten or dissolved ionic compound that conducts electricity
The electrode connected to the negative terminal

questions.explanation: The electrolyte is the molten or dissolved ionic compound that is decomposed during electrolysis. It conducts electricity because it contains free-moving ions that carry the charge.

questions.stem: During electrolysis, which electrode do positive ions (cations) move towards?

options.text: The cathode (negative electrode)
The anode (positive electrode)
They do not move during electrolysis
Both electrodes equally

questions.explanation: Positive ions (cations) are attracted to the cathode (negative electrode) because opposite charges attract. At the cathode, cations gain electrons (are reduced) to form atoms or molecules.

questions.stem: What happens to negative ions (anions) at the anode during electrolysis?

options.text: They dissolve into the solution
They lose electrons and are oxidised
They gain electrons and are reduced
Nothing happens to them

questions.explanation: At the anode (positive electrode), negative ions lose electrons and are oxidised. For example, chloride ions lose electrons to form chlorine gas: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

questions.stem: Which type of current must be used for electrolysis?

options.text: Alternating current (AC)
Either AC or DC
No current is needed
Direct current (DC)

questions.explanation: Direct current (DC) must be used for electrolysis so that each electrode maintains a constant charge (one always positive, one always negative). With alternating current, the polarity switches back and forth, so the ions would not migrate consistently to the correct electrode.

questions.stem: In electrolysis, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode. Which memory aid helps remember this?

options.text: PEMDAS
OIL RIG
ROY G BIV
OILRIG and PANIC (Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode)

questions.explanation: PANIC helps remember that the Positive electrode is the Anode and the Negative electrode Is the Cathode. Combined with OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons), you can work out what happens at each electrode.
